prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire flat bands

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B022, with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. The scientific content is a simple mechanism that can be written as a clean model. Moire interference between two graphene layers flattens the bands at a particular twist angle, which was a quantitative prediction in the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model. In 2018 correlated insulators and superconductivity appeared in the experiment at that angle, and many independent groups have since reproduced the phases. Round 1 did not shake the case that this is a new platform for tunable correlated matter, in which density and angle can be varied in one device. I want the citation to rest on what is established, namely the flat band and the existence of correlated and superconducting phases within it. It should not rest on any claim about the pairing mechanism. Written that way, the prize does not depend on the open question that worries Johansson and Lindroth.
statement.case_against: I keep the maturity objection against my own choice. The decisive experiment dates from 2018 and the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators are unresolved. Twist-angle disorder still limits sample-to-sample reproducibility. The credit is also incomplete: Cao and the other first authors of the 2018 papers cannot be named under the three-person limit, and the priority of the magic-angle condition relative to earlier moire band calculations has not been checked against the archive. B036 is the older, better settled and more widely supported case. Its real weakness is that it looks like a very large improvement within a line of metrology already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and I do not think that weakness is fatal. If the committee gives maturity priority over novelty of mechanism, B036 with Katori and Ye is a prize I could vote for without reservation about its scientific standing.

responses.point: Lindroth answers the overlap objection to B036 by saying the comb gave optical cycle counting and the ion work gave single-particle control, but neither gave a many-atom clock whose accuracy is not limited by the trap. She keeps B022 only as an alternative because the physics is remarkable but not ready, citing the unresolved pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder.
responses.response: Her answer to the overlap question is the most persuasive one given in round 1, and it changes my view of B036. The magic-wavelength condition is a clean statement about polarisabilities, which is the kind of universal mechanism I value, and it separates the lattice clock from the earlier prizes. The chair asked what objection keeps me from joining B036. It is now only a judgement about weighting. A citation built around the lattice architecture would read as a new idea and not as a continuation of the earlier prizes, and I would accept that. On B022 I disagree with 'not ready'. A prize for the flat band and the existence of the phases does not wait on the mechanism. Many groups have reproduced those phases over eight years. Disorder limits how well samples agree with each other, but the effect itself has not been contested, and the same was true when the quantum Hall effects were recognised.

responses.point: Johansson moved B036 to first after the opening ballots, ranks B022 at the bottom of his list because the discovery is recent, the pairing mechanism is open and twist-angle disorder limits reproducibility, and says the flat-band picture itself is stable.
responses.response: We agree on the facts, and our disagreement is only about how much weight maturity gets. The robustness question you raise is the right one. I would phrase it as a test: is the flat band and the correlated phase diagram seen in independent devices with different fabrication? It is, and the sample variation is in the details of the phases and not in their existence. That is why I would credit only the prediction and the observed phases. The chair asks what finding would change my view. It would be evidence that the correlated states are extrinsic to the flat band, for example that they are produced by strain or disorder, or that the continuum model fails to describe the band structure that the experiments measure. I know of no such evidence. If you judge that eight years is too short, I understand that. In that case I would prefer to see B036 go forward on its own and not see B022 diluted.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B022 first, accepts Bistritzer as co-credit, concedes B054 on the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit, and keeps B054 and B036 as safer options if interpretation must settle first.
responses.response: I agree with her on the allocation: the 2011 continuum model is a joint paper by Bistritzer and MacDonald, and the magic angle comes from that calculation, so the credit has to include Bistritzer. I also agree with her on B054. Its attribution has a visible gap while B022 has none on the supplied names. We both accept that Cao and the other 2018 authors cannot be named and that earlier twisted-graphene band theory could be argued as a precursor. I would not make B054 the fallback, because I would sooner fall back to B036 than to a prize whose credit list I think is incomplete. That is where we differ slightly.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B036 first as a mature, reproduced measurement technique with a clean Katori-Ye allocation, and leaves the pending redefinition of the second as an open question.
responses.response: I now accept his view of B036 on the merits, and I side with Johansson, Lindroth and Olsson on timing: the redefinition of the second is a standards process and should not decide a Nobel prize. On attribution, he and others note that Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow and the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups lie outside Katori and Ye. I cannot check the priority history from the record I have, and several of us admit to relying on memory. If the committee advances B036, someone with the archive in front of them should confirm it. A citation built on the lattice concept and the 10^-18 uncertainty would limit the damage to other groups.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will recognise the magic-angle flat band and the correlated and superconducting phases before the pairing mechanism is understood. I think it should and I cannot show that it will.

Exact priority of the magic-angle condition relative to earlier moire band theory, and whether the three-person limit fairly represents the experimental team of 2018. I am working from recollection and have not checked the archive.

Whether the many-atom lattice-clock architecture counts in the committee's eyes as a distinct achievement beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes. If it does, B036 is the stronger case on maturity and I would move to it.
Whether the credit for B036 is exactly Katori and Ye given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the other clock groups.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no known collaboration with any candidate on the shortlist, including MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Katori and Ye. I work in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson, with no documented collaboration, and this does not bear on any shortlisted candidate. I am a field outsider on B022, B036 and B046 alike, and my judgement on them is based on the general physics and not on specialist knowledge of the literature.
